introduction: “Rights should be equal,” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá told his Western audiences, and also: “absolute equality is a mere dream.” He was speaking in the years when socialism was the urgent question, and these readings give his answer to it. People differ in capacity; a society, like an army or a body, needs many functions; so degrees must remain. What must go is the extreme of wealth and poverty, the denial of equal rights, and any sense of superiority, and what should come is muvását, a voluntary sharing “higher than equality.” The analogies are ancient. Paul’s body with many members, Plato’s metals, the Qur’án’s “raised some of them above others in rank,” and Shakespeare’s speech on degree all say that difference of function is natural. The trouble is that every one of them has been used to defend privilege, and the outside quotations include the protests: John Ball’s rhyme, Burns’s “guinea stamp,” Rousseau’s chains, the Declaration of Independence. Aristotle’s sentence about natural rulers shows what the argument from nature can become. The last reading and Jesus’s “he that is chief, as he that doth serve” mark the difference.
questions: “Rights should be equal” and “the different degrees must persist.” Which equalities do the readings require, and which do they call impossible?
The readings compare society to an army and to a body. What does each comparison bring out, and where could each mislead?
Aristotle and others argued from natural difference to natural rule. What in these readings forbids that step?
Muvását, voluntary sharing, “is higher than equality.” Why higher? What does compulsion lose?
“The rank is but the guinea stamp.” In your own work, how would you tell respect for a function from deference to a person?

outside.why: “Gradations of rank are without doubt one of the essentials of society.” Shakespeare’s Ulysses: take but degree away, untune that string, and, hark, what discord follows!

The rebel priest of 1381 asked where rank came from: when Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman? What kind of rank do the readings defend, and what kind would they agree with John Ball in rejecting?
A system that “will preserve the various ranks. Every rank should perform its duties.” Paul: having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, let us wait on our ministering.
“Rights should be equal.” The American Declaration: all men are created equal; endowed with certain unalienable rights. In what are people equal, on the readings’ account, and in what are they not?

“An artisan remains an artisan; a merchant, a merchant … a ruler, a ruler.” Plato’s founding tale for his city: you are brothers, yet God has framed you differently; in some he has mingled gold, in others silver, brass and iron.
“Observe the human body, its limbs, its members.” Paul uses the same picture: if the whole body were an eye, where were the hearing?
And draws the same conclusion about regard: the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee.

A difference in degree and capacity, “not a matter of good or evil.” The parable of the talents: unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability.
“In the world of humanity there must needs be degrees.” The Qur’án: We have raised some of them above others in rank that some of them may take labour from others.
Humanity as an army in which not all can be officers. Menenius, calming a hungry crowd, told the fable of the body’s members that rebelled against the belly.

It does not mean all are equal; yet rich and poor “will all be at ease.” Pope: Order is heav’n’s first law; and, this confess’d, some are, and must be, greater than the rest; but who infers from hence that such are happier, shocks all common sense.
A king appoints minister, general and soldier. Paul finds the same variety in the heavens: one star differeth from another star in glory.
Burns on what a king’s appointments are worth: the rank is but the guinea stamp; the man’s the gowd for a’ that. Do the readings honour the stamp or the gold?
“Each is honored in his own place.” Proverbs: the rich and poor meet together: the Lord is the maker of them all.

“Absolute equality is a mere dream and impracticable.” Rousseau began from the opposite observation: man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains. What inequalities would Rousseau call chains that the readings would also condemn?
An organization is needed “which will bring about an order.” Aristotle’s proposal: the best political community is formed by citizens of the middle class.

“People cannot be equal because they are different in their creation.” Aristotle used differences of nature to justify permanent rule of one class of persons over another: the one rules, and the other is ruled. How do the readings prevent their argument from being used as his was?
Minister, commander, secretary: “all benefit from the sovereign’s favors.” Job on his servants: did not he that made me in the womb make him?

Without workers and craftsmen “the affairs and order of the world would be suspended.” Ben Sira on smiths and potters: without these cannot a city be inhabited; they will maintain the state of the world.
Voluntary sharing, muvását, “is higher than equality.” The first believers: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
“All things ought not to have been equal”; ask only whether each is sufficient in itself. Pope: vast chain of being, which from God began.
Ranks are preserved, and superiority is forbidden. Jesus: he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
